questions.question: A developer's prompt tells Claude to 'respond in exactly 50 words' to keep replies short and fast, but response lengths vary widely. Which change is most likely to give more reliable length control?

options.text: Set max_tokens to 50 so generation stops at exactly 50 words.
Repeat the word-count instruction in both the system prompt and the user turn.
Ask for a fixed number of sentences or paragraphs instead of a word count.
Ask Claude to count its words and append the total at the end of each reply.

questions.explanation: Because LLMs work in tokens rather than words, Anthropic notes that exact word-count limits are less effective than sentence or paragraph limits. max_tokens counts tokens, not words, and simply truncates the reply, often mid-sentence. Repeating the instruction doesn't fix the token-versus-word mismatch, and asking for a word tally adds output without actually limiting length.

questions.question: A team is moving a workload from an older Claude model to Claude Opus 4.7 or a later model. Their cost and context-fit estimates reuse token counts measured on the older model for the same prompts. What should they do?

options.text: Recount with the token counting endpoint and the new model ID, as its tokenizer may differ.
Keep the existing counts, since identical text produces identical token counts on every Claude model.
Estimate tokens from character counts using one fixed characters-per-token ratio for all models.
Reuse the old counts but reduce them by a flat percentage, since newer tokenizers are more compact.

questions.explanation: Claude 4.7 and later models use a newer tokenizer that produces roughly 30 percent more tokens for the same text, so the docs say to recount against the model you plan to use. Token counts are not identical across models, and no single characters-per-token ratio holds for every model and language. A flat reduction is backwards, because the newer tokenizer usually produces more tokens, not fewer.

questions.question: A support chatbot appends every user and assistant turn to the messages array. After long sessions, requests start failing with a 400 invalid_request_error saying the prompt is too long. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The max_tokens value is set lower than the length of the latest user message.
The API automatically drops earlier turns once a fixed turn count is passed.
Cached system prompt tokens count double toward the context window.
Accumulated history, system prompt, and tools now exceed the context window.

questions.explanation: Everything in the request counts toward the context window, including the system prompt, every message, and the tool definitions. Turns keep piling up, and once the input alone exceeds the window the API returns a 400 'prompt is too long' error. The API doesn't drop old turns for you (only chat interfaces may do that), and cached prefixes take up space only once. max_tokens limits the output, so it has nothing to do with how long the user's message is.

questions.question: A report-generation feature sends short prompts of about 500 tokens and receives responses of about 6,000 tokens. Finance asks where cost reduction efforts should focus. Which reasoning is correct?

options.text: Shorten the prompts, because input tokens are priced higher than output tokens.
Shorten the responses, because output tokens cost more per token and dominate here.
Neither matters, because Claude usage is billed per request rather than per token.
Enable prompt caching, because cache hits also lower the price of the generated output tokens.

questions.explanation: Claude is billed per million input tokens and per million output tokens, and output tokens cost several times more than input tokens on every current model. With 12 times more output than input, cutting response length gives the biggest savings. Billing is per token, not per request, and prompt caching reduces only the cost of input that is read from the cache, not output.

questions.question: A team is building a browser chat UI that shows Claude's answers as they are generated. A developer proposes opening a WebSocket from the browser straight to the Claude API with the API key embedded in the page. What should the team do instead?

options.text: Open a WebSocket from the backend to the Claude API, since token streaming needs a persistent socket.
Have the browser poll the Messages API every second with stream set to false to fetch partial text.
Call the API from the browser with the TypeScript SDK defaults, which keep the key hidden from users.
Have the backend call the API with stream true over SSE and relay those events to the browser.

questions.explanation: The Messages API streams responses with server-sent events over HTTP when stream is true, so a backend that holds the API key can consume that stream and forward the events to the browser over its own channel. No WebSocket endpoint is needed or documented for Messages API streaming. Polling with stream false does not return partial text, because a non-streaming call returns only the complete message. The TypeScript SDK disables browser use by default to avoid exposing credentials, and enabling dangerouslyAllowBrowser puts the secret key in client-side code where users can extract it.

questions.question: Users of a chat app complain that the screen stays blank for several seconds before a long answer appears all at once. The product team is satisfied with total generation time. Which change best addresses the complaint?

options.text: Move chat requests to the Message Batches API so responses are processed faster.
Increase max_tokens so the model has more room and finishes sooner.
Enable streaming and render text as it arrives to improve perceived speed.
Raise the temperature so the model commits to its first tokens faster.

questions.explanation: Streaming sends the response as it is generated, so users see text within about the time to first token instead of waiting for the full reply. This greatly improves perceived responsiveness. Batches are asynchronous and not meant for interactive use. A larger max_tokens doesn't make generation faster, and temperature controls randomness, not how quickly the first token arrives.

questions.question: A developer needs to reduce end-to-end latency for a high-volume feature that returns short product summaries. Output quality is already acceptable. Which TWO actions directly reduce latency? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Use a faster model tier, such as Haiku, after evaluations confirm quality holds.
Add several more detailed examples to the prompt to guide the formatting.
Raise max_tokens far above the expected length to avoid any truncation.
Instruct Claude to be concise so that fewer output tokens are generated.
Move the requests from the Messages API to the Message Batches API.

questions.explanation: Anthropic's latency guide lists choosing the right model, with Haiku as the fastest tier, and reducing prompt and output length as direct ways to cut latency. Adding examples makes the input longer. A higher max_tokens doesn't speed up generation. The Batches API is asynchronous and can take up to 24 hours, so it trades latency for cost.

questions.question: A developer uses the Anthropic SDK with a very large max_tokens value to generate long reports in a non-streaming call, and the SDK refuses the request to avoid an HTTP timeout. The developer doesn't need incremental text. What should they do?

options.text: Split each report into many separate requests that each use a small max_tokens.
Use the SDK's streaming helper and collect the final complete Message object.
Call the token counting endpoint first so capacity is reserved for the request.
Set temperature to 0 so that generation completes in fewer total tokens.

questions.explanation: The SDKs can stream internally and still return the same complete Message that a normal create call does. The docs note the SDK requires this for large max_tokens values to avoid HTTP timeouts. Splitting reports adds complexity and can break coherence. Token counting doesn't reserve any capacity, and temperature doesn't reliably shorten output.

questions.question: A developer tracks output tokens for streamed responses by adding up the usage.output_tokens value from each message_delta event. The resulting totals are higher than the billed usage. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: message_delta events report only input tokens, so the values are mislabeled.
ping events also carry usage fields, and those are being added into the running total.
The usage counts in message_delta events are cumulative, so summing double-counts.
Streamed responses get a discount that the event data does not reflect.

questions.explanation: The streaming docs say the token counts in a message_delta event's usage field are cumulative. Adding them up across events counts the same tokens more than once, so the developer should read the last value instead. message_delta does report output tokens, ping events carry no usage data, and streaming has no billing discount.

questions.question: A team's regression tests call a Claude model that accepts the temperature parameter, set temperature to 0, and assert that the output exactly matches a stored string. The tests fail intermittently. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: Temperature 0 applies only to the first token, and later tokens are sampled randomly.
The API caches outputs for identical inputs, and that cache has expired.
Temperature 0 makes the model choose randomly among its top candidate tokens.
Even at temperature 0, outputs are not fully deterministic across API calls.

questions.explanation: Anthropic's glossary says that even with temperature set to 0, results are not fully deterministic, and identical inputs can produce different outputs across API calls. Tests should therefore check structure or meaning rather than exact strings. Temperature applies to every sampled token, the API does not cache outputs this way, and lower temperature makes sampling more conservative, not more random.

questions.question: A Python service wants to slow its own request rate before it hits 429 errors by reading the anthropic-ratelimit-* headers on each Messages API response. Calls currently use client.messages.create, which returns only the parsed Message. What should the developer do?

options.text: Read the values from message.usage, where the SDK copies every rate-limit response header.
Call client.messages.with_raw_response.create, read headers, then call parse() for the Message.
Set default_headers on the client so the API echoes the rate-limit values in the Message body.
Turn on debug logging and parse the rate-limit header values out of the SDK's log output.

questions.explanation: The Python SDK exposes the underlying HTTP response through the .with_raw_response property, which returns an APIResponse whose headers can be read, and parse() returns the same object messages.create would have returned. The usage field reports token counts, not HTTP headers. default_headers controls headers the SDK sends on requests; it does not change what the API returns in the body. Scraping debug logs is fragile, and debug logging can expose request and response bodies.

questions.question: A team runs a code-refactoring assistant on Claude Opus 5.5. Responses are long, and users say answers take too long to finish streaming once they start. The team will pay more per token but wants no change in answer quality. Which approach fits?

options.text: Set speed to "fast", which routes the request to a smaller distilled variant of Opus that responds sooner.
Submit the requests through the Message Batches API with speed set to "fast" for faster and cheaper output.
Set speed to "fast" on the request, which runs the same model faster at premium per-token pricing.
Set speed to "fast" to cut time to first token, since fast mode mainly reduces the initial wait.

questions.explanation: Fast mode is requested with speed: "fast" and runs the same model with a faster inference configuration, giving up to 2.5x higher output tokens per second at premium pricing (for Claude Opus 5.5, $8 input / $40 output per MTok); Opus 5.5 no longer needs the fast-mode beta header. It is not a different or smaller model: the weights and behavior are the same, so quality does not change. Fast mode is not available with the Batch API. Its gains are focused on output tokens per second rather than time to first token, which is why it suits long streamed answers.

questions.question: A backend drives a Claude Managed Agents session. It sends a user.message event and then opens the session's event stream, but it sometimes misses the agent's first events. A teammate suggests switching to a WebSocket. What should the developer do?

options.text: Open the SSE event stream before sending events, and on reconnect merge in the listed event history.
Switch to the Managed Agents WebSocket endpoint, which replays every event from the session's start.
Read the missed events from the webhook endpoint, since webhook deliveries form a durable event log.
Send the user.message over the open stream connection, since the stream accepts events in both directions.

questions.explanation: Managed Agents sessions stream events over server-sent events (accept: text/event-stream), and events you send are posted separately to the session's events endpoint. A stream delivers only events emitted after it opens, so the docs say to open the stream before sending events; to reconnect, open a new stream, list the event history to seed seen IDs, and skip duplicates while tailing. The docs describe no WebSocket endpoint for this. Webhooks only notify of major state changes, carry just a type and ID, and are explicitly not a durable log, and sending happens by POST rather than over the stream.

questions.question: A team registers a Console webhook endpoint for Claude Managed Agents session events so it can update a status dashboard without polling. Which TWO practices should the webhook handler follow? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Apply events in arrival order, since deliveries are guaranteed to match the order events occurred.
Deduplicate on the top-level event.id, because retried deliveries carry the same event ID.
Return a 3xx redirect when the dashboard moves, so Anthropic follows it to the new endpoint URL.
Treat each delivery body as a full resource snapshot and skip extra API calls to stay fast.
Verify the signature, then fetch the referenced resource with a GET call to read its state.

questions.explanation: Webhook deliveries can repeat, and every attempt carries the same top-level event.id, so handlers should deduplicate on it. Payloads contain only the event type and ID rather than the full object, so after verifying the signature (for example with the SDK's unwrap() helper) the handler fetches the resource with a GET call. Ordering is explicitly not guaranteed, so state should be driven by the fetched resource rather than arrival order. A 3xx response disables the endpoint immediately because redirects are never followed.

questions.question: A user asks a Claude-based assistant about a regulation enacted after the model's reliable knowledge cutoff, and the answer is outdated. What is the best way to make such answers current?

options.text: Retrieve the current regulation text at request time and include it in the prompt.
Lower the temperature so the model recalls its most recent training data first.
Tell the model in the system prompt to assume that today's date is the current date.
Raise the effort level so the model can reason its way to more recent facts.

questions.explanation: Retrieval augmented generation fetches relevant information at runtime and passes it into the context window. This lets the model use information beyond its training data, which is especially useful when up-to-date information is needed. Temperature and effort can't add knowledge the model never learned. Telling it today's date doesn't supply the missing facts either.

questions.question: A developer moves an app from Claude Opus 4.5 to Claude Opus 4.8. The request still sends thinking type "enabled" with budget_tokens set to 16000, and the API now returns a 400 error. What should the developer do?

options.text: Remove budget_tokens, set thinking type to "adaptive", and steer depth with output_config effort.
Keep type "enabled" but lower budget_tokens to 1,024, the largest budget newer models accept.
Add the interleaved-thinking beta header, which re-enables manual budget_tokens thinking on 4.8.
Set effort to "adaptive" inside the thinking object so the model picks its own thinking budget.

questions.explanation: Claude 4.7 and later models reject manual extended thinking (type "enabled" with budget_tokens) with a 400 error; the documented migration is to remove budget_tokens, set thinking to {type: "adaptive"}, and control reasoning depth with output_config.effort. With adaptive thinking Claude decides per request whether and how much to think, so it may skip thinking on easy inputs. Changing the budget value does not help because the enabled type itself is unsupported, and 1,024 is the documented minimum budget, not a maximum. The interleaved-thinking header has no manual-mode effect on 4.7 and later models. "adaptive" is a thinking mode, not an effort level, and effort lives in output_config rather than inside the thinking object.

questions.question: A new engineer asks why Claude follows instructions well when its underlying model was pretrained only to predict the next word in text. Which explanation is accurate?

options.text: Next-word pretraining alone makes models naturally excellent at following instructions.
The pretrained model was refined with fine-tuning and RLHF to act as an assistant.
Claude looks up instruction-following rules in an external database at inference time.
Each API request fine-tunes the model's weights on the instructions it receives.

questions.explanation: Anthropic's glossary explains that pretrained autoregressive models predict the next word and are not inherently good at following instructions. Fine-tuning and RLHF refine them into helpful assistants. Instruction following doesn't come from an external rule database, and inference requests don't change the model's weights.

questions.question: A developer's data-extraction prompt describes the desired output format only in prose, and responses come back in inconsistent formats. Which change is most likely to improve consistency?

options.text: Add a sentence stressing that following the format is extremely important.
Raise the temperature so Claude converges on the most common format.
Add 3 to 5 diverse, relevant examples wrapped in example tags.
Add a single example and tell Claude to copy it exactly for every input.

questions.explanation: Anthropic calls examples (few-shot or multishot prompting) one of the most reliable ways to steer output format. The examples should be relevant, diverse, wrapped in example tags, and ideally number 3 to 5. Emphasis words don't show Claude what the format looks like. Higher temperature makes output more varied, not more consistent. A single example copied exactly risks overfitting to that one case.

questions.question: A team runs two Claude workloads: a tagger that labels the sentiment of short reviews, and an agent that debugs multi-file test failures. They want to spend reasoning tokens where they pay off most. Which configuration is most appropriate?

options.text: High effort for the tagger and low effort for the debugger, since short inputs need more reasoning.
Maximum effort for both workloads, since added reasoning improves every task equally.
The lowest effort for both workloads, since effort only changes response formatting.
Low effort for the tagger and a higher effort level for the debugging agent.

questions.explanation: Thinking helps most on complex tasks such as coding, analysis, and long agentic work. Anthropic recommends low effort for simple, speed-sensitive tasks and higher effort for complex reasoning and difficult coding. Option A has it backwards. Maximum effort everywhere wastes tokens on easy work, and effort affects all output tokens, including thinking and tool calls, not just formatting.

questions.question: With thinking enabled and display set to 'summarized', a developer notices usage.output_tokens is much larger than the visible thinking summary plus the final answer. What explains the difference?

options.text: Billing covers the full thinking tokens generated, not the shorter summary returned.
Thinking tokens are billed twice, once as input and once as output, on the same turn.
The summary is written by the target model as an extra pass billed as more output.
The output count also includes system prompt tokens that the API echoes back.

questions.explanation: With summarized thinking, you are charged for the full thinking tokens the request generated, not for the summary tokens, so the billed output count won't match what you see. The summary is produced by a different model, not as an extra billed pass of the target model. Thinking tokens are billed once as output when generated, and system prompt tokens are input that is never echoed back.

questions.question: On an older model that supports manual extended thinking, a developer sends thinking type 'enabled' with budget_tokens 8000 and max_tokens 4000, without interleaved thinking. The API rejects the request. What is the correct fix?

options.text: Lower budget_tokens to 500 so that thinking uses fewer tokens than the reply.
Set max_tokens above budget_tokens, since thinking counts toward max_tokens.
Remove max_tokens, since it cannot be combined with extended thinking requests.
Move budget_tokens into output_config, where thinking budgets must be specified.

questions.explanation: budget_tokens must be at least 1,024 and less than max_tokens, because thinking tokens count toward the max_tokens limit for the turn. Interleaved thinking is the only exception. A budget of 500 is below the minimum and would also be rejected. max_tokens is still required, and budget_tokens belongs in the thinking object, not in output_config.

questions.question: A platform team hard-codes each Claude model's context window and output limit in a config file, and the values keep going stale as new models launch. They want the app to discover models and their limits at runtime. What should they do?

options.text: Parse each model ID string, since the ID encodes the model's context window and output limit.
Send a tiny Messages request to each model and infer its limits from any error text returned.
Call GET /v1/models and read max_input_tokens, max_tokens, and capabilities for each model.
Call GET /v1/models with lifecycle omitted, which lists every model including retired ones.

questions.explanation: The Models API (GET /v1/models) lists available models, newest first, and its response includes max_input_tokens, max_tokens, and a capabilities object for each model, so limits can be read at runtime instead of hard-coded. Model IDs identify a model and version but do not encode its token limits. Probing with test requests and parsing error text is slow, costly, and brittle. When lifecycle is omitted the list contains only active and deprecated models; retired models appear only when requested explicitly.

questions.question: A developer adds cache_control to a system prompt of about 300 tokens. Requests succeed, but cache_creation_input_tokens and cache_read_input_tokens are both 0 on every call. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: cache_control must be placed on the first user message rather than the system prompt.
Caching works only with the 1-hour TTL, and the default setting caches nothing.
The API rejected the cache_control block and reported the error in a response header.
The prompt is below the model's minimum cacheable length, so it is processed uncached.

questions.explanation: Every model has a minimum cacheable prompt length. Shorter prompts are processed without caching and no error is returned, and both cache usage fields being 0 shows that nothing was cached. Breakpoints can go on system prompt blocks, and the default 5-minute TTL does cache content. There is no hidden error header for this case.

questions.question: A team caches a long system prompt and its tool definitions, but cache_read_input_tokens is always 0 even though requests arrive seconds apart. Which TWO issues would explain this? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: The user's question changes each request and sits after the cache breakpoint.
The responses are streamed instead of being returned in a single payload.
The system prompt begins with a timestamp that changes on every request.
The cache breakpoint is placed on the final block of the system prompt.
The tool definitions are regenerated in a different order on each request.

questions.explanation: Cache matching is exact, byte for byte, up to the breakpoint, in the order tools, then system, then messages. Any change to tool definitions invalidates the whole cache, and a changing timestamp early in the system prompt breaks the prefix match. Content after the breakpoint can change freely. Streaming doesn't affect caching, and placing a breakpoint at the end of the system prompt is the normal setup.

questions.question: A developer creates a Message Batch over raw HTTP and immediately tries to download its results, but the batch's results_url is null. How should the code collect the results?

options.text: Re-create the batch with stream set to true on each request so the results arrive as server-sent events.
Call the cancel endpoint, which finalizes the batch early and fills in results_url right away.
Poll the retrieve endpoint until processing_status is "ended", then stream the JSONL at results_url.
Read each request's output from request_counts in the create response, which holds the results.

questions.explanation: A Message Batch starts with processing_status "in_progress" and moves to "ended" once all requests finish, so the client polls the retrieve endpoint and then downloads results from results_url, which serves a .jsonl file the docs recommend streaming. Batch requests are processed asynchronously and are not streamed back as server-sent events. Canceling stops unprocessed requests rather than producing their results. request_counts only reports how many requests reached each state, not their outputs.

questions.question: A backfill script builds a single Message Batches create request holding about 90,000 requests whose JSON body totals roughly 400 MB. The call fails immediately with HTTP 413 request_too_large, and retrying produces the same error. What should the developer do?

options.text: Retry with exponential backoff, because 413 means the batch endpoint is temporarily overloaded
Split the work into several batches, each under 256 MB and 100,000 requests
Send the requests through the Messages API instead, because it accepts larger request bodies
Request a higher usage tier, since 413 means the organization's batch quota has been used up

questions.explanation: A 413 request_too_large error means the request body exceeds the endpoint's maximum size, and a single Message Batch is limited to 100,000 requests or 256 MB, whichever is reached first, so the payload must be split across several batches. Retrying an oversized request unchanged fails the same way; 413 is not a transient condition like 529 overloaded_error. The Messages API has a smaller limit (32 MB per request), not a larger one. Quota and spend-cap problems are reported as 429 rate_limit_error, not 413.

questions.question: Before sending user-uploaded documents to Claude, a developer wants each request's input size so that very long documents can be routed differently and kept within the context window. Which approach fits best?

options.text: Send each document to the Messages API with max_tokens 1 and read its usage.
Divide each document's character count by a constant that works on all models.
Call the token counting endpoint, which is free and accepts message-shaped input.
Query the Models API, which returns a token count for any text you supply.

questions.explanation: The token counting endpoint accepts the same structured inputs as a message, including system prompts, tools, images, and PDFs. It is free to use, has its own rate limits, and the docs specifically list routing decisions and context-window fit as uses. Its count is an estimate. Real Messages calls cost money, a fixed character ratio ignores tokenizer differences, and the Models API returns model limits, not counts for your text.

questions.question: A developer submitted a large Message Batch with the wrong prompt and calls the cancel endpoint while the batch is still in progress. What should the developer expect?

options.text: The batch and every result produced so far are deleted at once and can no longer be retrieved later.
The batch enters canceling; in-progress requests may still finish, so check each request's result.
Every request stops at once, and the whole batch is billed at the standard non-batch request rate.
The call is rejected, because a batch cannot be stopped once any request has begun processing.

questions.explanation: Batches can be canceled any time before processing ends; the batch enters a canceling state, and the system may complete in-progress, non-interruptible requests before finalizing. request_counts shows how many were canceled, and the individual results show which ones, with canceled requests not billed. Cancel does not delete the batch or its finished results; deletion is a separate endpoint. Cancellation is allowed while processing is under way, so it is not rejected.

questions.question: A company requires all outbound traffic from its Python service to pass through a corporate HTTP proxy. The service calls Claude with the Anthropic Python SDK. How should the developer configure this?

options.text: Pass a client from the separate httpx package with a proxy set, since any httpx client is accepted.
Pass http_client=DefaultHttpxClient(proxy=...) to the client so the SDK's defaults are kept.
Set base_url to the proxy's address so the SDK tunnels each request through it to the API.
Add a proxy field to extra_body on each request so the API routes the call through the proxy.

questions.explanation: The Python SDK sends requests with httpx2, and proxies and transports are customized by passing an http_client; the docs recommend DefaultHttpxClient so default settings such as timeouts and connection limits are preserved. A client from the separate httpx package raises a TypeError. base_url (or ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL) changes which server the SDK treats as the API, not the proxy it travels through. extra_body adds fields to the JSON request body sent to the API and does not affect network routing.

questions.question: A developer's dashboard reads anthropic-ratelimit-tokens-remaining and anthropic-ratelimit-tokens-reset from each response. The team assumes capacity drops to zero and refills all at once at the reset time each minute. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: The reset header gives seconds to wait, and the remaining value is exact down to a single token.
These headers always show the organization-level limit, even when a workspace limit is lower.
Capacity refills in one step at the reset time, so requests should be held until that moment.
Capacity refills continuously; reset is an RFC 3339 time when the limit is fully replenished.

questions.explanation: The API uses a token bucket, so capacity is replenished continuously up to the maximum rather than reset at fixed intervals, and the -reset headers give the RFC 3339 time when the limit will be fully replenished. The remaining token values are rounded to the nearest thousand, and the seconds-to-wait value comes from the retry-after header instead. The anthropic-ratelimit-tokens-* headers show the most restrictive limit in effect, such as a workspace limit. Holding all requests until the reset time wastes capacity that is already refilling.

questions.question: A team is considering moving a production workload from a larger Claude model to a cheaper one to reduce costs. What should they do first?

options.text: Switch all traffic and monitor customer complaints to detect any regressions.
Compare public benchmark leaderboards and pick the cheaper model if it is close.
Build a benchmark from their real prompts and data and compare quality and edge cases.
Ask the cheaper model to rate its own confidence on a few sample prompts first.

questions.explanation: Anthropic says a good evaluation set built for your use case is the most important step when deciding whether to change models. Test with your actual prompts and data, compare accuracy, quality, and edge-case handling, then weigh performance against cost. Watching complaints finds regressions too late, public benchmarks may not reflect your workload, and a model's self-rated confidence isn't a reliable measure.

questions.question: A coding pipeline has a reliable automated test suite that checks every output, and running all tasks at high effort is expensive. Which strategy did Anthropic find cut cost while keeping the same pass rate?

options.text: Run every task at maximum effort but cap max_tokens tightly to limit total spend.
Route each task randomly between two models and keep the first output returned.
Run every task twice at low effort and keep the longer of the two outputs.
Run all tasks at low effort and re-run only the failing ones at high effort.

questions.explanation: Anthropic's cost guidance describes running everything at low effort and re-running only failures at high effort. This was about 40% cheaper than running everything at high effort at the same pass rate, but it needs a reliable checker. Tight max_tokens caps cause truncation, random routing ignores task difficulty, and output length is not a quality signal.

questions.question: A team running a single Claude model wants to lower costs and is considering an executor/advisor setup that pairs a smaller executor with a frontier advisor model. According to Anthropic's guidance, what should they do first?

options.text: Sweep effort levels on the current model, and build a pairing only if it beats that curve.
Deploy the advisor pairing right away, since consulting an advisor always raises scores.
Replace the current model with the frontier advisor model for every single request.
Add the advisor tool to all requests, since it adds no cost when it is not consulted.

questions.explanation: Anthropic advises tuning one model before adding a second. Sweep effort on the current model first, and build a pairing only if it beats that model's score-versus-spend curve. In Anthropic's tests, advisor gains varied and sometimes vanished when the advisor was rarely consulted. Moving everything to the frontier model raises cost, and the advisor's tool definition adds roughly 1,000 prompt tokens per request even when it's never used.

questions.question: A team is comparing two Claude model tiers for an agentic workload before deciding which to put into production. Which TWO evaluation practices does Anthropic recommend? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Compare the tiers on price per million tokens, since that sets total workload cost.
Measure cost per completed task using outcome checks such as tests passing.
Evaluate mainly on the easiest tasks, since they make up most of the traffic.
Use production tasks weighted like real traffic, including the hardest tail.
Rely on overall impressions from a handful of manually reviewed conversations.

questions.explanation: Anthropic recommends comparing models on cost per completed task with outcome checks, using production tasks weighted like real traffic, and paying close attention to the hardest tasks, because that tail drives spend. Price per token ignores how many tokens and retries each model needs to finish a task. Easy-task-only evaluation and informal impressions both miss the cases that decide quality and cost.

questions.question: A developer writes a manual agentic loop with the Messages API and client-side tools. The agent sometimes stops after its first tool call and never delivers a final answer, because the loop exits as soon as the response contains any content block. Which loop condition should the developer use?

options.text: Keep looping while stop_reason is "tool_use": run the tools, return tool_result blocks, and exit on any other value.
Keep looping until the response contains at least one text block, then treat that text block as Claude's final answer to the user.
Keep looping while stop_reason is "end_turn", because that value signals Claude wants another round of tool execution.
Keep looping for a fixed number of requests and concatenate every text block returned along the way into the final answer.

questions.explanation: The canonical client-tool loop is keyed on stop_reason: while it is "tool_use", run the requested tools, return tool_result blocks, and call again; any other value (end_turn, max_tokens, stop_sequence, refusal) exits the loop. Text blocks often accompany tool_use blocks, so their presence does not mean the turn is finished. "end_turn" means Claude is done, not that it wants more tools. A fixed request count ignores what Claude actually asked for.

questions.question: A team is building a loan-approval workflow in LangGraph as an explicit graph: fetch the application, score risk, wait for a human underwriter, then notify the applicant. The approval wait can last days and must survive server restarts, resuming exactly where it paused. Which approach should the team use?

options.text: Store graph state in a module-level variable and have the approval node poll a database flag in a sleep loop until it flips.
Call interrupt() in the approval node, then resume with Command(resume=...) under a fresh thread_id so the run starts clean.
Compile with a durable checkpointer, call interrupt() in the approval node, and resume with Command(resume=...) on the same thread_id.
Compile the graph without a checkpointer and, once the underwriter approves, rerun the entire graph from its start node.

questions.explanation: LangGraph's interrupt() pauses graph execution inside a node and relies on a checkpointer to persist state, so a durable checkpointer is needed in production for the pause to survive restarts. The run is resumed by invoking the graph with a Command whose resume value becomes the return value of interrupt(), using the same thread_id that identifies the saved state. A fresh thread_id starts a new thread with empty state, so the paused run is never resumed. In-memory polling loops lose state on restart and tie up a worker, and running without a checkpointer means there is nothing to resume, forcing the whole workflow (including risk scoring) to run again. Note that on resume the interrupted node restarts from its beginning, so code before interrupt() should be safe to re-run.

questions.question: A developer uses PydanticAI with Agent('anthropic:claude-sonnet-5-5') to extract invoice fields. Downstream code needs a validated Invoice Pydantic object, and when Claude returns data that fails validation or a business rule, the framework should ask the model to try again. Which approach fits PydanticAI's design?

options.text: Set output_type=Invoice on the Agent and add an @agent.output_validator that raises ModelRetry when a business rule fails.
Keep the default string output, then call Invoice.model_validate on the text and silently drop any results that fail validation.
Describe the Invoice fields in the system prompt and extract each value from the reply text with regular expressions in your code.
Set a high temperature in AnthropicModelSettings so Claude explores more candidate outputs until one happens to validate.

questions.explanation: PydanticAI's output_type accepts a Pydantic model; the framework builds a JSON schema from it (by default using Claude's tool calling) and validates what the model returns. Output validators registered with @agent.output_validator can apply extra checks, and raising ModelRetry sends the error back so the model tries again, consuming the run's output retry budget. Validating a free-text string afterward and discarding failures loses the automatic retry loop, and regex extraction from prose gives no schema validation at all. Raising temperature does not make output conform to a schema; it only adds randomness.

questions.question: A team runs a supervisor research agent that delegates to specialist worker subagents. Broad questions such as comparing every vendor in a market improve a lot, but simple lookups like a single company's founding year now spawn many subagents and burn tokens. Based on Anthropic's multi-agent research system lessons, what should the team change?

options.text: Remove the supervisor and route every query, broad or narrow, to one agent so token usage is the same for all requests.
Have the supervisor always spawn a fixed number of subagents so per-query cost stays predictable for the finance team.
Let each worker subagent spawn its own sub-workers so simple lookups finish faster through deeper delegation layers.
Add effort-scaling rules to the supervisor prompt: one agent for simple facts, more subagents as complexity grows.

questions.explanation: Anthropic found agents struggle to judge appropriate effort, so it embedded scaling rules in the lead agent's prompt: simple fact-finding needs one agent with 3-10 tool calls, direct comparisons 2-4 subagents, and complex research more than 10 subagents with divided responsibilities. A supervisor hierarchy helps on breadth-first queries because subagents work in parallel with their own context windows, but multi-agent systems use far more tokens, so it should be used only where it pays off. Removing the hierarchy would lose the large gains on broad research, and a fixed subagent count keeps overspending on simple lookups. Adding deeper delegation layers increases cost and coordination overhead rather than reducing it.

questions.question: A Python Claude Agent SDK app must guarantee that no Bash command containing "DROP TABLE" ever runs. A system prompt instruction forbidding it was ignored once in testing. Which approach enforces the rule deterministically?

options.text: Rewrite the system prompt rule in capital letters, repeat it at the end of the prompt, and add examples of refused commands.
Register a PreToolUse hook for Bash that returns permissionDecision "deny" with a reason in hookSpecificOutput.
Register a PostToolUse hook for Bash that sets permissionDecision to "deny" whenever the executed command contains DROP TABLE.
Register a PreToolUse hook for Bash that returns an empty object {} for matching commands so that the SDK blocks the call.

questions.explanation: Agent SDK hooks are callbacks that run your code at execution points, so a PreToolUse hook with matcher "Bash" fires before every Bash call regardless of what the model decides. Returning hookSpecificOutput with hookEventName, permissionDecision "deny", and a permissionDecisionReason blocks the call and tells Claude why. Prompt wording, however emphatic, is a request the model may not follow, not enforcement. PostToolUse fires after the tool has already run, so it can log or add context but cannot prevent the command, and returning {} from a hook allows the operation unchanged.

questions.question: A team uses the Anthropic client SDK's Tool Runner so they don't have to write the tool loop themselves. A new requirement says a human must approve every issue_refund call before it executes, and every decision must be logged. According to Anthropic's documentation, what is the recommended approach?

options.text: Set max_iterations to 1 on the Tool Runner so each refund call pauses and waits for approval before continuing.
Switch to a manual tool-use loop, which the docs recommend for human-in-the-loop approval and custom logging.
Keep the Tool Runner unchanged and add a system prompt asking Claude to get approval before issuing refunds.
Mark the refund tool as strict so the Tool Runner automatically pauses and asks a human before running it.

questions.explanation: The Tool Runner docs say it handles the loop, error wrapping, and type safety for you, but for human-in-the-loop approval, custom logging, or conditional execution you should use the manual loop. max_iterations only caps the number of loop iterations; it adds no approval step. A prompt instruction is not an enforced control. strict: true guarantees the input matches the schema and has nothing to do with approvals.

questions.question: A team runs a Claude Agent SDK query that often spawns several subagents. Finance wants a hard ceiling on the estimated spend of each run, including subagent work. Which configuration meets this requirement?

options.text: Set maxTurns on the main query; subagent turns count toward it, so the turn cap also caps total spend.
Set effort to "low" so the main agent and all of its subagents consume fewer tokens.
Set maxBudgetUsd; subagent spend counts toward the cap, and the run ends with error_max_budget_usd.
Set CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONCURRENT_SUBAGENTS to 1 so that only one subagent can ever run during the query.

questions.explanation: maxBudgetUsd / max_budget_usd caps estimated spend. The docs state that subagent spend counts toward it, that spawning further subagents fails once the cap is reached, and that the query ends with the error_max_budget_usd subtype. maxTurns counts tool-use round trips, not dollars. Lower effort reduces tokens but sets no ceiling. Limiting concurrency affects how many subagents run at once, not total cost.

questions.question: A CI job runs a Claude Agent SDK query with maxTurns set to 30 to fix failing tests. On a large refactor, the ResultMessage comes back with subtype "error_max_turns". The team wants to finish the task without repeating the work already done. What should they do?

options.text: Read the result field of the ResultMessage, which holds the partial fix, and apply it before starting a new session.
Start a fresh query with the same prompt and maxTurns removed, so the agent can finish everything in a single run.
Fork the session with forkSession so the new branch gets a reset turn counter and a restored copy of the files.
Capture the session_id from the ResultMessage and resume that session with a higher maxTurns to continue the work.

questions.explanation: Every ResultMessage subtype carries session_id, and the docs suggest recovering from error_max_turns by resuming the session with a higher limit, which restores the prior context. The result field is only present on the success subtype. A fresh query throws away the context already built up. Forking branches the conversation history but does not snapshot or restore files.

questions.question: In an isolated container, a developer configures a Claude Agent SDK agent with permissionMode "bypassPermissions" and allowedTools ["Read", "Grep"], expecting the agent to be unable to run shell commands. During testing, the agent runs Bash anyway. How should the developer prevent Bash from being used?

options.text: Add "Bash" to disallowedTools, which removes the tool from the request and is enforced even in bypassPermissions.
Add "Bash" to allowedTools with an empty specifier, which tells bypassPermissions that the tool is not approved.
Move "Read" and "Grep" to the front of allowedTools, because bypassPermissions only approves the first entries.
Switch permissionMode to "acceptEdits", which approves only the tools in allowedTools and blocks every other tool.

questions.explanation: allowedTools only pre-approves the tools it lists. Unlisted tools fall through to the permission mode, and bypassPermissions approves them, so allowedTools does not constrain that mode. A bare-name disallowedTools entry removes the tool definition so Claude can't attempt it, and deny rules apply even in bypassPermissions. List order has no effect. acceptEdits auto-approves file operations; it does not limit the agent to the allowedTools list.

questions.question: A team deploys a headless Claude Agent SDK agent with no human available to answer permission prompts. They want a fixed, explicit tool surface: Read, Glob, and Grep should run, and anything else that would normally prompt should be refused outright instead of left waiting. Which configuration fits best?

options.text: Set allowedTools to the three tools and permissionMode to "plan" so every other tool call is denied automatically.
Set allowedTools to the three tools and permissionMode to "dontAsk" so any call that would prompt is denied.
Set allowedTools to the three tools and permissionMode to "default" with no canUseTool callback registered.
Set allowedTools to the three tools and permissionMode to "bypassPermissions" so that no prompts ever appear.

questions.explanation: The docs recommend pairing allowedTools with permissionMode "dontAsk" for a locked-down agent: listed tools are approved, and any call that would otherwise prompt is denied without calling canUseTool. Plan mode is for exploring and proposing changes, and it sends edits to canUseTool. Relying on default mode with no callback is the "silent reliance" on canUseTool being absent that dontAsk is meant to replace. bypassPermissions approves every unlisted tool.

questions.question: A startup wants Claude to run data-migration tasks that take hours and involve many shell commands and file edits. They don't want to build or operate their own agent loop, sandbox, or tool execution layer, and they need server-side conversation history they can fetch later. Which Anthropic offering fits best?

options.text: The Messages API with a custom agent loop, since direct model prompting is best for long-running asynchronous work.
The client SDK Tool Runner, which hosts tool execution and sandboxed shell access on Anthropic's infrastructure.
Claude Managed Agents, a hosted harness that runs the loop in a managed sandbox and persists event history.
The Message Batches API, which runs each long migration as an asynchronous batch job with tools executed for you.

questions.explanation: Claude Managed Agents is a pre-built, configurable agent harness running on managed infrastructure, aimed at long-running tasks and asynchronous work. It provides sandboxed Bash and file tools and persists event history server-side. The Messages API is for custom loops and fine-grained control, which the team wants to avoid. Tool Runner runs your tools in your own process. Batches is for asynchronous bulk requests and provides no agent harness or sandbox.

questions.question: A developer uses Claude Agent SDK sessions to let users explore two alternative refactoring approaches from the same starting analysis. Which TWO statements about sessions are accurate? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Forking a session creates a new session ID with a copy of the history, and the original session stays unchanged.
Forking a session also snapshots the working directory, so file edits in the fork are invisible to the original.
Resuming a session restores the conversation and also reverts files the agent changed after that point.
Sessions persist the conversation, not files; file checkpointing is the feature for reverting file changes.
Continue requires passing a session ID, while resume automatically picks the most recent session in the directory.

questions.explanation: A fork gets its own session ID, starts from a copy of the original history, and leaves the original untouched. Sessions persist conversation history, not files; reverting file changes requires file checkpointing. File edits in a fork are real and visible to any session using the same directory, and resume does not revert files. It's the other way around for continue and resume: continue finds the most recent session, and resume takes a specific ID.

questions.question: A content team generates long policy documents. The task always splits into the same fixed steps: draft an outline, confirm the outline covers every required section, then write the full document from the outline. They are willing to trade some latency for accuracy. Which pattern from Anthropic's "Building effective agents" fits best?

options.text: Routing, with a classifier that sends each request to either an outlining prompt or a full-drafting prompt.
Orchestrator-workers, with a central LLM deciding at runtime which sections to delegate to worker LLMs.
Parallelization by voting, running the drafting prompt several times and keeping the most common result.
Prompt chaining, where each call uses the previous output and a programmatic gate checks the outline.

questions.explanation: Prompt chaining splits a task into a fixed sequence of LLM calls, and programmatic "gates" on intermediate steps keep it on track. Anthropic gives outline, check against criteria, then write as an example. Routing classifies inputs into different paths, but every request here follows the same path. Orchestrator-workers is for subtasks that can't be predicted ahead of time. Voting repeats one task for confidence and doesn't model sequential steps.

questions.question: A support platform receives general questions, refund requests, and technical issues. Each category needs different prompts and tools, and categories can be classified accurately. The team also wants simple questions handled by a smaller, cheaper model. Which workflow pattern should they use?

options.text: Routing: classify each input and send it to a specialized follow-up prompt or model for its category.
Prompt chaining: pass every query through general, refund, and technical prompts one after another.
Evaluator-optimizer: have one model answer and a second critique the answer until it reaches target quality.
Parallelization by sectioning: send every query to all three category prompts at once and merge them.

questions.explanation: Routing classifies an input and directs it to a specialized follow-up task. It works well when distinct categories are better handled separately and can be classified accurately, and Anthropic's examples include customer-service query types and sending easy questions to smaller, cheaper models. Running every query through all category prompts, in sequence or in parallel, wastes cost and mixes concerns. Evaluator-optimizer improves quality through iteration and doesn't send work to specialized paths.

questions.question: A chatbot team finds that asking one Claude call to both screen user input for inappropriate requests and answer the question performs worse than expected. Which approach does Anthropic's "Building effective agents" suggest for this case?

options.text: Prompt chaining, where the answer is generated first and a second call screens it before display.
Parallelization by sectioning, where one instance screens the input while another generates the response.
Parallelization by voting, where several identical calls each answer and screen, and the majority wins.
An autonomous agent that decides on each turn whether a guardrail check is needed for the request.

questions.explanation: Anthropic gives guardrails as an example of sectioning: one model instance processes the user query while another screens it, which tends to work better than one call doing both. The chaining option screens only after the answer is generated, and it adds latency in sequence. Voting runs the same combined task several times instead of separating the concerns. Letting an autonomous agent decide whether to apply a guardrail removes a check that should always run.

questions.question: A security team wants higher confidence when Claude flags vulnerabilities in pull requests. They plan to review the same code with several different prompts and flag it if enough reviews report a problem. Which pattern is this?

options.text: Routing, because each prompt specializes in a different category of vulnerability for the code.
Evaluator-optimizer, because each prompt grades the previous review and asks for improvements.
Parallelization by voting, running the same task several times to get diverse outputs to aggregate.
Orchestrator-workers, because a lead model plans the review and delegates files to worker models.

questions.explanation: Voting is the form of parallelization where the same task runs multiple times to get diverse outputs, and reviewing code for vulnerabilities with several prompts is one of Anthropic's examples. Routing sends each input down one path rather than gathering several judgments. Evaluator-optimizer is an iterative generate-and-critique loop. Orchestrator-workers splits the work dynamically into different subtasks instead of repeating the same one.

questions.question: A team builds a coding assistant that applies feature requests across a codebase. The number of files and the kind of change in each depend entirely on the request, so subtasks can't be defined in advance. Which pattern fits best, and how does it differ from parallelization?

options.text: Prompt chaining, which differs from parallelization by running predefined subtasks in a fixed order.
Routing, which differs from parallelization by sending each file to the single most suitable model.
Evaluator-optimizer, which differs from parallelization by refining each file edit through repeated critiques.
Orchestrator-workers, which differs from parallelization because the orchestrator sets subtasks per input.

questions.explanation: In orchestrator-workers, a central LLM breaks the task down dynamically, delegates subtasks to workers, and synthesizes their results. Anthropic names coding changes across multiple files as an example. Its key difference from parallelization is that subtasks are determined by the orchestrator for each input instead of being predefined. Chaining and routing both depend on paths defined in advance. Evaluator-optimizer refines output quality but does not decompose an unpredictable task.

questions.question: A publisher uses Claude for literary translation. First drafts miss nuances that an expert reviewer can clearly articulate, and revisions based on that feedback measurably improve quality. Which pattern should they adopt?

options.text: Evaluator-optimizer: one LLM call translates and another evaluates and gives feedback, in a loop.
Routing: classify each passage by genre and send it to a translation prompt for that genre.
Parallelization by sectioning: split the text into chapters and translate them all at once.
Prompt chaining: translate the text, then run a second call that formats the output for print.

questions.explanation: Evaluator-optimizer works best when evaluation criteria are clear and iterative refinement adds measurable value. Literary translation with nuance-focused critiques is Anthropic's own example. Routing by genre does not add a feedback loop. Sectioning by chapter speeds things up but does not improve nuance. A formatting step afterward does not evaluate or revise the translation.

questions.question: An insurance company processes claims through well-defined steps that rarely vary, and auditors need predictable, consistent behavior. A developer proposes an autonomous agent that decides its own steps and tool calls. Based on Anthropic's guidance, what should the team choose?

options.text: An autonomous agent, because agents always beat predefined code paths once tools are added.
A workflow with predefined code paths, which gives predictability for well-defined tasks.
A multi-agent system, because splitting claims across agents makes behavior more consistent.
An autonomous agent with no turn limit, so it can work through every claim in a single run.

questions.explanation: Anthropic distinguishes workflows, where LLMs and tools are orchestrated through predefined code paths, from agents, where the LLM directs its own process. Workflows offer predictability and consistency for well-defined tasks, while agents suit cases that need flexible, model-driven decisions. Agents trade higher cost and latency for flexibility and don't automatically perform better. Adding more agents increases variability and cost. Removing turn limits takes away an important control.

questions.question: A team wants Claude to answer questions about internal HR policies. A prototype that makes a single Claude call with retrieved policy passages and a few in-context examples already meets their accuracy target. Someone suggests building an orchestrator with planning subagents. What does Anthropic's guidance recommend?

options.text: Build the orchestrator now, since agentic systems become cheaper per query as usage grows over time.
Replace retrieval with an autonomous browsing agent so that answers are not limited to retrieved passages.
Keep the single optimized LLM call and add agentic complexity only if it is shown to improve outcomes.
Add an evaluator-optimizer loop on every answer, because all production systems require iterative refinement.

questions.explanation: Anthropic advises starting with the simplest solution and adding complexity only when needed. Optimizing a single LLM call with retrieval and in-context examples is often enough, and agentic systems trade latency and cost for better task performance. Agentic systems don't get cheaper per query with scale. Autonomous browsing adds risk and cost with no stated need. Evaluator-optimizer is useful only when iteration adds measurable value, not as a default.

questions.question: A developer adopts an agent framework and finds it hard to debug because the abstraction layers hide the exact prompts and responses being sent to Claude. What does Anthropic recommend in "Building effective agents"?

options.text: Add a second framework on top to provide the logging that the first framework's abstractions hide.
Avoid any framework entirely, since frameworks are incompatible with agentic patterns on Claude.
Keep the framework but move all logic into one large prompt so fewer layers are involved overall.
Start with direct LLM API calls, and if a framework is used, make sure to understand its code.

questions.explanation: Anthropic warns that frameworks can add abstraction layers that obscure the underlying prompts and responses, making systems harder to debug. Its advice is to start with LLM APIs directly, since many patterns take only a few lines, and to understand the underlying code if you use a framework. Stacking frameworks makes the problem worse. Anthropic does not call frameworks incompatible; it lists several, including the Claude Agent SDK. Cramming everything into one prompt does not fix the visibility problem.

questions.question: A team is preparing an autonomous coding agent for production. Its steps can't be predicted in advance, and errors could compound across many iterations. Based on Anthropic's "Building effective agents", which TWO practices should they adopt? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Have the agent skip environment feedback between steps, relying only on its own initial plan to save tokens.
Include stopping conditions such as a maximum number of iterations to keep the agent under control.
Remove all human checkpoints, since pausing for feedback undermines the benefits of agent autonomy.
Deploy straight to production with broad permissions, since extensive testing cannot capture agent behavior.
Test extensively in sandboxed environments with appropriate guardrails before trusting the agent's autonomy.

questions.explanation: Anthropic notes that autonomous agents usually stop when the task is complete, but stopping conditions such as a maximum number of iterations help maintain control. Because autonomy raises costs and allows errors to compound, it recommends extensive testing in sandboxed environments with appropriate guardrails. Agents should gather ground truth from the environment at each step, such as tool results, not ignore it. Human checkpoints and pausing when blocked are explicitly part of the design. Skipping testing goes against the guidance.

questions.question: A team wants to turn its single-agent coding assistant into a multi-agent system. Most of their tasks are coding changes with tight dependencies between steps, and every agent would need the same shared context. According to Anthropic's write-up of its multi-agent research system, what is the most appropriate conclusion?

options.text: Multi-agent is likely a poor fit: it uses far more tokens and suits parallelizable, high-value tasks.
Multi-agent is ideal here, because shared context and tight dependencies are where subagents work best.
Multi-agent will cut token usage compared with a single agent, so it is the cheaper option for coding.
Multi-agent should be adopted, because it outperforms single agents on every task type by roughly 90%.

questions.explanation: Anthropic reports that multi-agent systems use about 15x the tokens of chat interactions and fit valuable tasks with heavy parallelization. Domains where all agents need the same context, or where there are many dependencies between agents, are a poor fit, and Anthropic says most coding tasks have fewer truly parallelizable parts than research. The 90.2% improvement was measured on Anthropic's internal research eval, not on every task type. Multi-agent systems raise token use; they don't lower it.

questions.question: A Claude Agent SDK agent has to survey dozens of files to find every place a deprecated API is used, then make a focused fix. The main conversation's context fills with file contents before it reaches the fix. Which change addresses this most directly?

options.text: Raise maxTurns so the main agent has more round trips available before the context window fills up.
Delegate the survey to a subagent that runs in its own context and returns only its final message.
Put the full file list in the system prompt so the main agent never needs to read the files.
Set permissionMode to "plan" so file reads are summarized automatically before entering the context.

questions.explanation: Subagents provide context isolation. Each runs in its own fresh conversation, its intermediate tool calls and results stay inside it, and only its final message goes back to the parent, so the main context grows by a summary rather than the full transcript. More turns don't add context space. A file list doesn't give the agent the file contents it needs. Plan mode prevents edits; it doesn't summarize reads.

questions.question: In a Claude Agent SDK app, the main agent discusses a stack trace and the relevant file paths with the user, then delegates the fix to a custom subagent. The subagent starts by searching for information the user already gave. What is the most likely cause, and the fix?

options.text: The subagent's model differs from the parent's; set model to "inherit" so it shares the parent's conversation.
The subagent lacks the Read tool; add Read to its tools list so it can access the parent's earlier messages.
A non-fork subagent doesn't get the parent's history; include paths and errors in the Agent tool's prompt.
The session wasn't resumed; pass resume with the session ID so the subagent loads the parent's transcript.

questions.explanation: The docs say a non-fork subagent starts with a fresh context and does not receive the parent's conversation history or tool results. The only parent-to-subagent channel is the Agent tool's prompt string, so file paths, error messages, and decisions must be included there. The model setting controls which model runs, not what context is shared. Read accesses files, not the parent conversation. Resume restores a session for a new query; it does not pass parent context to a subagent.

questions.question: In an orchestrator-worker research system, the lead agent gives subagents short instructions like "research the semiconductor shortage". Subagents duplicate each other's searches and leave gaps. Based on Anthropic's multi-agent research system lessons, what should the team change?

options.text: Give every subagent the lead agent's entire conversation history so each one can infer what the others are doing.
Replace the subagents with one large agent that runs every search in sequence inside a single context window.
Raise the number of subagents spawned per query so that the gaps get covered by the additional overlap.
Have the lead give each subagent an objective, output format, tool and source guidance, and clear boundaries.

questions.explanation: Anthropic found that short, vague task descriptions led subagents to misinterpret tasks or duplicate work. Each subagent needs an objective, an output format, guidance on tools and sources, and clear task boundaries. Sharing the full history defeats context isolation and adds token cost. Going back to a single sequential agent gives up the parallelism benefits. Adding subagents without better instructions only increases duplication and cost.

questions.question: A long-running Claude Agent SDK agent is told in its initial prompt to "never modify files under migrations/". After many turns, automatic compaction runs, and the agent later edits a migration file. What is the recommended way to make this rule persist?

options.text: Put the rule in CLAUDE.md loaded through settingSources, because that content is re-injected on every request.
Repeat the rule in the initial prompt several times, so the compaction summary is more likely to retain it.
Disable compaction by raising maxTurns, so the agent's context window never reaches its size limit.
Fork the session after each compaction, so the fork restores the original uncompacted first prompt.

questions.explanation: Compaction replaces older messages with a summary, so instructions from early in a conversation may be lost. The docs recommend putting persistent rules in CLAUDE.md (loaded via settingSources) because that content is re-injected on every request. A hard enforcement such as a deny rule or PreToolUse hook is also an option. Repeating the instruction doesn't guarantee it survives summarization. maxTurns limits round trips and doesn't control compaction. A fork copies the current history, which is already compacted.

questions.question: A team runs long-lived, stateful research agents in production. Restarting a run after a mid-task failure is expensive and frustrating for users, and code deployments occasionally break agents that are in progress. Which TWO practices from Anthropic's multi-agent research system address these problems? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Restart every failed agent from the beginning so that each run starts again from a clean, known state.
Deploy all agent code updates at once to every running instance so that no old version stays active.
Let agents resume from where the error occurred, combining retry logic with regular checkpoints.
Hide tool failures from the agent so that it continues on its original plan without changing course.
Use rainbow deployments that shift traffic gradually while old and new versions run side by side.

questions.explanation: Anthropic describes building systems that can resume from where an error occurred instead of restarting, combined with retry logic and regular checkpoints. To avoid breaking agents in progress, it uses rainbow deployments that gradually shift traffic from old to new versions while both keep running. Restarting from scratch is exactly the expensive outcome the team wants to avoid. Replacing all versions at once breaks running agents. Anthropic suggests letting agents know when a tool is failing so they can adapt, not hiding failures.

questions.question: In a multi-agent system, subagents produce large artifacts such as code files and detailed reports. Passing each artifact back through the lead agent's context costs many tokens and loses detail when the lead rewrites it. What approach does Anthropic describe for this?

options.text: Have each subagent compress its artifact into a one-line summary that the lead later expands back into full detail.
Merge all subagents into the lead agent, so the artifacts are produced directly inside the lead's own context.
Have subagents write outputs to an external system such as a filesystem and pass lightweight references to the lead.
Raise the lead agent's max_tokens so it can repeat every subagent artifact verbatim in its final synthesis output.

questions.explanation: Anthropic describes letting subagents store their work in external systems and pass lightweight references back to the coordinator. This avoids information loss from multi-stage processing and cuts token overhead from copying large outputs through conversation history. One-line summaries lose the very detail being protected. Merging everything into the lead gives up context isolation. Raising max_tokens still routes everything through the lead's context, so the token cost remains.

questions.question: A developer's prompt reads only "Create an analytics dashboard." Claude returns a bare-bones result, while the product team expected a feature-rich implementation. Following Anthropic's guidance on being clear and direct, what should the developer do?

options.text: Raise the temperature so that Claude explores more creative and ambitious implementations.
State the expectation explicitly, e.g. ask for many relevant features beyond the basics.
Keep the prompt short and trust Claude to infer the team's expectations from the task name.
Add the instruction "Do not produce a minimal dashboard" in capitals for emphasis.

questions.explanation: Anthropic's guidance says that if you want above-and-beyond behavior you should request it explicitly rather than rely on Claude to infer it from a vague prompt; its own example adds "Include as many relevant features and interactions as possible." Temperature does not supply missing requirements, a short prompt is the cause of the problem, and the docs recommend saying what to do rather than what not to do.

questions.question: A voice assistant's system prompt includes the rule "NEVER use ellipses," but Claude still occasionally uses similar punctuation that the speech engine mispronounces. Which revision best follows Anthropic's prompting guidance?

options.text: Repeat the rule three times in different sections of the system prompt to reinforce it.
Move the rule into the user turn so that it is closer to the generated response.
Replace the rule with a long list of every punctuation mark that is not allowed.
Explain that output goes to a text-to-speech engine that cannot pronounce ellipses.

questions.explanation: Anthropic recommends giving the context or motivation behind an instruction; its example rewrites "NEVER use ellipses" to explain the text-to-speech constraint, and notes Claude is smart enough to generalize from the explanation. Repetition, relocation, or an exhaustive blocklist do not convey the underlying reason, so Claude cannot generalize to similar cases.

questions.question: A company is building an internal assistant that must answer consistently in the voice of a senior tax specialist across every conversation. Where should the developer establish this role?

options.text: In the system prompt, for example a sentence such as "You are a senior tax specialist."
In a prefilled assistant turn that begins every response with the specialist's full job title.
In the tool descriptions, so the role is attached to each tool Claude might call.
In a stop sequence, so Claude halts whenever it drifts out of the specialist persona.

questions.explanation: Anthropic's guidance is to set a role in the system prompt to focus Claude's behavior and tone, noting that even a single sentence makes a difference. Prefilling the last assistant turn is not supported on Claude 4.6 and later models, tool descriptions describe tools rather than persona, and stop sequences only end generation.

questions.question: A contract-review prompt concatenates instructions, background on the client, sample clauses, and the contract text as plain paragraphs. Claude sometimes treats sample clauses as part of the contract. What is the most effective fix?

options.text: Shorten the instructions so that the contract text makes up a larger share of the prompt.
Send each section as a separate API request and merge Claude's answers in application code.
Wrap each content type in its own XML tag, e.g. <instructions>, <examples>, <contract>.
Put the entire prompt in the system parameter so Claude treats it as authoritative.

questions.explanation: Anthropic recommends XML tags when a prompt mixes instructions, context, examples, and variable inputs; wrapping each type in its own tag reduces misinterpretation. Shortening instructions or moving everything into the system prompt does not separate the content types, and splitting into separate requests loses the context Claude needs to review the contract.

questions.question: A support-ticket summarizer includes one example summary in its prompt. Claude now copies that example's length and opening phrase for every ticket, even very different ones. According to Anthropic's multishot guidance, what should the developer do?

options.text: Remove all examples and rely on a longer written description of the format instead.
Move the single example into the system prompt so it is treated as guidance, not a template.
Duplicate the same example several times so Claude treats it as a firm standard.
Provide 3-5 relevant, diverse examples wrapped in <example> tags within <examples>.

questions.explanation: Anthropic advises examples that are relevant, diverse enough that Claude does not pick up unintended patterns, and structured in <example>/<examples> tags, with 3-5 examples for best results. Removing examples discards one of the most reliable steering tools, relocating one example does not fix the overfitting, and duplicating it reinforces the unwanted pattern.

questions.question: A developer is running a multi-step pricing calculation with thinking turned off. They want Claude to work through the problem before answering, while their code extracts only the final number. Which prompt approach matches Anthropic's guidance?

options.text: Instruct Claude to answer immediately with only the number so no reasoning tokens are spent.
Ask Claude to reason through the problem first, then put the final answer in <answer> tags.
Provide a strict stop sequence of "Answer:" so the response ends before any reasoning appears.
Ask for the number first and the reasoning afterward so the parser can stop at the first line.

questions.explanation: As a fallback when thinking is off, Anthropic suggests asking Claude to think through the problem before answering and to put the final answer in <answer> tags so it can be extracted. Answering immediately removes the reasoning, a stop sequence on "Answer:" would cut off the very answer you need, and reasoning after the answer cannot improve that answer.

questions.question: A team upgrades an extraction service to a Claude 4.6-generation model. Their old code ended each request with an assistant message containing "{" to force JSON output, and requests now fail with a 400 error. What is the recommended migration?

options.text: Move the "{" prefill into the system prompt so that it is sent as an instruction instead.
Keep the prefill but add a second empty assistant message after it to satisfy validation.
Remove the prefill and use the Structured Outputs feature to constrain the JSON schema.
Switch to stop_sequences of "}" so Claude stops once it closes the JSON object.
